{{Short description|Event spreading an infectious disease}}
[[File:Hotel Metropole 9th floor layout SARS 2003.svg|thumbnail|right|9th floor layout of the Hotel Metropole in [[Hong Kong]], showing where a superspreading event of [[severe acute respiratory syndrome]] (SARS) occurred in 2003]]
A '''superspreading event''' ('''SSEV''') is an event in which an [[infectious disease]] is spread much more than usual, while an unusually contagious organism [[infection|infected]] with a [[pathogen|disease]] is known as a '''superspreader'''. In the [[human-to-human transmission|context of a human-borne illness]], a superspreader is an individual who is more likely to infect others, compared with a typical infected person. Such superspreaders are of particular concern in [[epidemiology]].

Some cases of superspreading conform to the [[80/20 rule]],<ref name="galvani05">{{cite journal | vauthors = Galvani AP, May RM | title = Epidemiology: dimensions of superspreading | journal = Nature | volume = 438 | issue = 7066 | pages = 293–295 | date = November 2005 | pmid = 16292292 | pmc = 7095140 | doi = 10.1038/438293a | bibcode = 2005Natur.438..293G }}</ref> where approximately 20% of infected individuals are responsible for 80% of transmissions, although superspreading can still be said to occur when superspreaders account for a higher or lower percentage of transmissions.<ref name="Lloyd-Smith JO 2005">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lloyd-Smith JO, Schreiber SJ, Kopp PE, Getz WM | title = Superspreading and the effect of individual variation on disease emergence | journal = Nature | volume = 438 | issue = 7066 | pages = 355–359 | date = November 2005 | pmid = 16292310 | pmc = 7094981 | doi = 10.1038/nature04153 | bibcode = 2005Natur.438..355L }}</ref>  In [[epidemic]]s with such superspreader events, the majority of individuals infect relatively few [[contact tracing|secondary contacts]].{{citation needed|date=May 2020}} The degree to which superspreading contributes to an epidemic is often quantified by the ''t<sub>20</sub>'' metric, which denotes the proportion of infections attributable to the most infectious 20% of the population.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = von Csefalvay C  | chapter = Chapter 3: Host factors: Who gets sick and why |date= January 2023 |title = Computational Modeling of Infectious Disease |pages=93–119 | veditors = von Csefalvay C |publisher=Academic Press |language=en |doi=10.1016/b978-0-32-395389-4.00012-8 |isbn=978-0-323-95389-4 }}</ref>

SSEVs are shaped by multiple factors including a decline in [[herd immunity]], [[nosocomial infection]]s, [[virulence]], [[viral load]], [[misdiagnosis]], [[Droplet infection|airflow dynamics]], [[immune suppression]], and [[co-infection]] with another [[pathogen]].<ref name=stein11>{{cite journal | vauthors = Stein RA | title = Super-spreaders in infectious diseases | journal = International Journal of Infectious Diseases | volume = 15 | issue = 8 | pages = e510–e513 | date = August 2011 | pmid = 21737332 | pmc = 7110524 | doi = 10.1016/j.ijid.2010.06.020 | quote = The minority of individuals who infect disproportionately more susceptible contacts, as compared to most individuals who infect few or no others, became known as super-spreaders, and their existence is deeply rooted in history: between 1900 and 1907, Typhoid Mary infected 51 individuals, three of whom died, even though she only had an asymptomatic infection. | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Definition==

Although loose definitions of superspreader events exist, some effort has been made at defining what qualifies as a superspreader event (SSEV). Lloyd-Smith et al. (2005) define a protocol to identify a superspreader event as follows:<ref name="Lloyd-Smith JO 2005"/>
# estimate the effective reproductive number, ''R'', for the disease and population in question;
# construct a [[Poisson distribution]] with mean ''R'', representing the expected range of ''Z'' due to [[stochasticity]] without individual variation;
# define an SSEV as any infected person who infects more than ''Z<sup>(n)</sup> others'', where ''Z<sup>(n)</sup>'' is the nth percentile of the Poisson(''R'') distribution.

This protocol defines a 99th-percentile SSEV as a case which causes more infections than would occur in 99% of infectious histories in a homogeneous population.<ref name="Lloyd-Smith JO 2005"/>

During the [[SARS-CoV-1]] [[2002–2004 SARS outbreak]] from China, epidemiologists defined a superspreader as an individual with at least eight transmissions of the disease.<ref name="shen03">{{cite journal | vauthors = Shen Z, Ning F, Zhou W, He X, Lin C, Chin DP, Zhu Z, Schuchat A | display-authors = 6 | title = Superspreading SARS events, Beijing, 2003 | journal = Emerging Infectious Diseases | volume = 10 | issue = 2 | pages = 256–260 | date = February 2004 | pmid = 15030693 | pmc = 3322930 | doi = 10.3201/eid1002.030732 }}</ref>

Superspreaders may or may not show any symptoms of the disease.<ref name=stein11/><ref name=cory13>{{cite book| vauthors = Wiley DC, Cory AC |title=Encyclopedia of School Health|date=2013|publisher=Sage|location=Los Angeles, CA|isbn=978-1412996006 |quote=Historically, one of the most famous examples of super-spreading was that of Mary Mallon, better known as Typhoid Mary, who infected many contacts, several of whom died, through food she prepared and consequently contaminated, even thought she did not show symptoms. }}</ref>

SSEVs can further be classified into 'societal' and 'isolated' events.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Majra D, Benson J, Pitts J, Stebbing J | title = SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) superspreader events | journal = The Journal of Infection | volume = 82 | issue = 1 | pages = 36–40 | date = January 2021 | pmid = 33245943 | pmc = 7685932 | doi = 10.1016/j.jinf.2020.11.021 }}</ref> Funerals have been known to epidemiology as common superspreader events. In particular where funeral rites involve contact with the decedent, funerary transmission may occur.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = von Csefalvay C | chapter = Chapter 2: Simple compartmental models: The bedrock of mathematical epidemiology |date= January 2023  | title =Computational Modeling of Infectious Disease |pages=19–91 | veditors = von Csefalvay C |publisher=Academic Press |language=en |doi=10.1016/b978-0-32-395389-4.00011-6 |isbn=978-0-323-95389-4 }}</ref> The [[International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement|International Red Cross]] proposed the practices now known as "safe and dignified burials" during the [[Western African Ebola virus epidemic]] to reduce funerary transmission.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sikakulya FK, Ilumbulumbu MK, Djuma SF, Bunduki GK, Sivulyamwenge AK, Jones MK | title = Safe and dignified burial of a deceased from a highly contagious infectious disease ebolavirus: Socio-cultural and anthropological implications in the Eastern DR Congo | journal = One Health | volume = 13 | article-number = 100309 | date = December 2021 | pmid = 34458545 | pmc = 8379334 | doi = 10.1016/j.onehlt.2021.100309 }}</ref>

In April 2020 [[Jonathan Kay]] reported in relation to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]:<ref name="jknp">{{cite news | vauthors = Kay J |title=It's not the size of the event, but the behaviour that matters |url=https://nationalpost.com/opinion/jonathan-kay-on-covid-19-its-not-the-size-of-the-event-but-behaviour-that-matters |publisher=National Post, a division of Postmedia Network Inc |date=30 April 2020}}</ref>
{{cquote|Putting aside hospitals, private residences and old-age homes, almost all of these superspreader events (SSEVs) took place in the context of (1) parties, (2) face-to-face professional networking events and meetings, (3) religious gatherings, (4) sports events, (5) meat-processing facilities, (6) ships at sea, (7) singing groups, and, yes, (8) funerals.}}

==Factors in transmission==
[[Image:Herd immunity.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|How an infection spreads in a community with immunized and non-immunized members.]]
Superspreaders have been identified who excrete a higher than normal number of pathogens during the time they are infectious. This causes their contacts to be exposed to higher viral/bacterial loads than would be seen in the contacts of non-superspreaders with the same duration of exposure.<ref name="Kenneth J. Rothman 2008. page 561">Kenneth J. Rothman, Sander Greenland, and Timothy L. Lash. ''Modern Epidemiology'', 3rd Edition. 2008. p. 561. Lippincott, Williams & Wilkins. Philadelphia.</ref>

===Basic reproductive number===
The [[basic reproduction number]] R<sub>0</sub> is the [[statistical mean|average]] number of secondary infections caused by a typical infective person in a totally susceptible population.<ref name="galvani05"/> The basic reproductive number is found by multiplying the average number of contacts by the average probability that a susceptible individual will become infected, which is called the shedding potential.<ref name="Lloyd-Smith JO 2005"/>

{{math|1=R<sub>0</sub> = Number of contacts × Shedding potential}}

===Individual reproductive number===
The individual reproductive number represents the number of secondary infections caused by a specific individual during the time that individual is infectious. Some individuals have significantly higher than average individual reproductive numbers and are known as superspreaders. Through [[contact tracing]], epidemiologists have identified superspreaders in [[measles]], [[tuberculosis]], [[rubella]], [[monkeypox]], [[smallpox]], [[Ebola]] hemorrhagic fever and [[SARS]].<ref name="Lloyd-Smith JO 2005"/><ref name=deserres13>{{cite journal | vauthors = De Serres G, Markowski F, Toth E, Landry M, Auger D, Mercier M, Bélanger P, Turmel B, Arruda H, Boulianne N, Ward BJ, Skowronski DM | display-authors = 6 | title = Largest measles epidemic in North America in a decade--Quebec, Canada, 2011: contribution of susceptibility, serendipity, and superspreading events | journal = The Journal of Infectious Diseases | volume = 207 | issue = 6 | pages = 990–998 | date = March 2013 | pmid = 23264672 | doi = 10.1093/infdis/jis923 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Co-infections with other pathogens===
Studies have shown that men with HIV who are co-infected with at least one other [[sexually transmitted disease]], such as [[gonorrhea]], [[hepatitis C]], and [[herpes simplex 2]] virus, have a higher HIV shedding rate than men without co-infection. This shedding rate was calculated in men with similar HIV viral loads. Once treatment for the co-infection has been completed, the HIV shedding rate returns to levels comparable to men without co-infection.<ref name=cohen97>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cohen MS, Hoffman IF, Royce RA, Kazembe P, Dyer JR, Daly CC, Zimba D, Vernazza PL, Maida M, Fiscus SA, Eron JJ | display-authors = 6 | title = Reduction of concentration of HIV-1 in semen after treatment of urethritis: implications for prevention of sexual transmission of HIV-1. AIDSCAP Malawi Research Group | journal = Lancet | volume = 349 | issue = 9069 | pages = 1868–1873 | date = June 1997 | pmid = 9217758 | doi = 10.1016/s0140-6736(97)02190-9 | s2cid = 9723768 }}</ref><ref name=winter99>{{cite journal | vauthors = Winter AJ, Taylor S, Workman J, White D, Ross JD, Swan AV, Pillay D | title = Asymptomatic urethritis and detection of HIV-1 RNA in seminal plasma | journal = Sexually Transmitted Infections | volume = 75 | issue = 4 | pages = 261–263 | date = August 1999 | pmid = 10615314 | pmc = 1758225 | doi = 10.1136/sti.75.4.261 }}</ref>

===Lack of herd immunity===
[[Herd immunity]], or herd effect, refers to the indirect protection that immunized community members provide to non-immunized members in preventing the spread of contagious disease. The greater the number of immunized individuals, the less likely an outbreak can occur because there are fewer susceptible contacts. In epidemiology, herd immunity is known as a ''dependent happening'' because it influences transmission over time. As a pathogen that confers immunity to the survivors moves through a susceptible population, the number of susceptible contacts declines. Even if susceptible individuals remain, their contacts are likely to be immunized, preventing any further spread of the infection.<ref name="Kenneth J. Rothman 2008. page 561"/><ref name="Fine P 1993">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fine PE | title = Herd immunity: history, theory, practice | journal = Epidemiologic Reviews | volume = 15 | issue = 2 | pages = 265–302 | year = 1993 | pmid = 8174658 | doi = 10.1093/oxfordjournals.epirev.a036121 }}</ref> The proportion of immune individuals in a population above which a disease may no longer persist is the ''herd immunity threshold''. Its value varies with the virulence of the disease, the efficacy of the vaccine, and the contact parameter for the population.<ref>{{cite book |veditors=Jamison DT, Breman JG, Measham AR |title=Priorities in Health: Disease Control Priorities Companion Volume |publisher=World Bank Publications |year=2006  |chapter=Chapter 4: Cost-Effective Strategies for the Excess Burden of Disease in Developing Countries<br />Section: Vaccine-preventable Diseases |chapter-url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK10258/#A151 |isbn=0-8213-6260-7}}</ref> That is not to say that an outbreak can't occur, but it will be limited.<ref name="Fine P 1993"/><ref name="yeung05">{{cite journal | vauthors = Yeung LF, Lurie P, Dayan G, Eduardo E, Britz PH, Redd SB, Papania MJ, Seward JF | display-authors = 6 | title = A limited measles outbreak in a highly vaccinated US boarding school | journal = Pediatrics | volume = 116 | issue = 6 | pages = 1287–1291 | date = December 2005 | pmid = 16322148 | doi = 10.1542/peds.2004-2718 | s2cid = 27236339 }}</ref><ref name="fine11">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fine P, Eames K, Heymann DL | title = "Herd immunity": a rough guide | journal = Clinical Infectious Diseases | volume = 52 | issue = 7 | pages = 911–916 | date = April 2011 | pmid = 21427399 | doi = 10.1093/cid/cir007 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Superspreaders during outbreaks or pandemics ==
===COVID-19 pandemic: 2020–present===
Several factors are identified as contributing to superspreading events with COVID-19: closed spaces with poor ventilation, crowds, and close contact settings ("three Cs").<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Enserink M, Kupferschmidt K, Desai N | date = February 2020 | title = The science of superspreading. | journal = Science Magazine |url = https://vis.sciencemag.org/covid-clusters/ }}</ref>

The South Korean spread of confirmed cases of [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2|SARS-CoV-2]] infection jumped suddenly starting on 19–20 February 2020. On 19 February, the number of confirmed cases increased by 20. On 20 February, 58<ref name=getnews>{{cite news |title=코로나19 확진자 104명...31번 환자 연관 신천지교회 대남병원서만 확진자 58명, 1명 사망 |url=https://m.getnews.co.kr/view.php?ud=2020022021135849202aaae0046f_16 |access-date=16 March 2020 |work=글로벌경제신문 |date=20 February 2020 |language=ko}}</ref> or 70<ref name="ThomReut_SKorea_zombie">{{cite news | vauthors = Shin H, Cha S | title= 'Like a zombie apocalypse': Residents on edge as coronavirus cases surge in South Korea |trans-title = <!-- trans-title is the English translation --> | date= 2020-02-20 |agency=[[Thomson Reuters]] | url= https://www.reuters.com/article/us-china-health-southkorea-cases/like-a-zombie-apocalypse-residents-on-edge-as-coronavirus-cases-surge-in-south-korea-idUSKBN20E04F |access-date=2020-02-20 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200220114624/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-china-health-southkorea-cases/like-a-zombie-apocalypse-residents-on-edge-as-coronavirus-cases-surge-in-south-korea-idUSKBN20E04F |archive-date= 2020-02-20 |url-status=live <!-- live|dead|unfit|usurped --> |url-access = <!-- (subscription/registration/limited) default=free -->}}</ref> new cases were confirmed, giving a total of 104 confirmed cases, according to the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Korea]] (KCDC). According to ''[[Reuters]]'', KCDC attributed the sudden jump to 70 cases linked to "Patient 31", who had participated in a gathering in [[Daegu]] at the [[Shincheonji Church of Jesus the Temple of the Tabernacle of the Testimony]].<ref name="ThomReut_SKorea_zombie" /> On 20 February, the streets of Daegu were empty in reaction to the Shincheonji outbreak. A resident described the reaction, stating "It's like someone dropped a bomb in the middle of the city. It looks like a zombie apocalypse."<ref name="ThomReut_SKorea_zombie" /> On 21 February, the first death was reported.<ref name=nbcsk>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/south-korea-reports-first-coronavirus-death-infections-linked-church-rise-n1139821 |title=South Korea reports first coronavirus death as infections linked to church rise|website=NBC News|date=20 February 2020 |language=en|access-date=2020-02-21}}</ref> According to the mayor of Daegu, the number of suspected cases as of 21 February is 544 among 4,400 examined followers of the church.<ref name=chosun>{{cite web |title=신천지 관련 확진자 76명으로 늘어...대구 교인 의심자만 544명 |publisher=Chosun.com |date=21 February 2020 |url=https://news.chosun.com/site/data/html_dir/2020/02/21/2020022101558.html}}</ref> Later in the outbreak, in May, a 29-year-old man visited several Seoul nightclubs in one night and resulted in accumulated infections of at least 79 other people.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://nwww.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20200511000575 |title= Itaewon cluster caseload rises to 79: Nation adds 35 new cases, 20 in Seoul |author= Park Han-na |date= 11 May 2020  |website= The Korea Herald |access-date= 11 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200516111911/http://nwww.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20200511000575 |archive-date=16 May 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref>

A two-day leadership conference for the American biotechnology company [[Biogen]] was held at the Marriott Long Wharf Hotel in [[COVID-19 pandemic in Boston|Boston, Massachusetts]], from 26 to 28 February 2020. 99 of the 175 executives in attendance later tested positive for COVID-19, and the hotel was shut down days later.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news | vauthors = Wines M |title=What Happens When a Superspreader Event Keeps Spreading |work=The New York Times |date=12 December 2020 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/11/us/biogen-conference-covid-spread.html |access-date=9 November 2022}}</ref> A genetic analysis study<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lemieux JE, Siddle KJ, Shaw BM, Loreth C, Schaffner SF, Gladden-Young A, Adams G, Fink T, Tomkins-Tinch CH, Krasilnikova LA, DeRuff KC, Rudy M, Bauer MR, Lagerborg KA, Normandin E, Chapman SB, Reilly SK, Anahtar MN, Lin AE, Carter A, Myhrvold C, Kemball ME, Chaluvadi S, Cusick C, Flowers K, Neumann A, Cerrato F, Farhat M, Slater D, Harris JB, Branda JA, Hooper D, Gaeta JM, Baggett TP, O'Connell J, Gnirke A, Lieberman TD, Philippakis A, Burns M, Brown CM, Luban J, Ryan ET, Turbett SE, LaRocque RC, Hanage WP, Gallagher GR, Madoff LC, Smole S, Pierce VM, Rosenberg E, Sabeti PC, Park DJ, MacInnis BL | display-authors = 6 | title = Phylogenetic analysis of SARS-CoV-2 in Boston highlights the impact of superspreading events | journal = Science | volume = 371 | issue = 6529 | date = February 2021 | pmid = 33303686 | pmc = 7857412 | doi = 10.1126/science.abe3261 }}</ref> published later the same year estimated the spread at the conference eventually resulted in 1.9% of U.S. coronavirus cases, or as many as 300,000 people. The event was the subject of a New York Times article,<ref name=":0" /> and substantial criticism was leveled at Biogen for its role in the incident.

Between 27 February and 1 March, [[2020 Tablighi Jamaat COVID-19 hotspot in Malaysia|a Tablighi Jamaat event]] at Masjid Jamek, Seri Petaling in [[Kuala Lumpur]], [[Malaysia]] attended by approximately 16,000 people resulted in a major outbreak across the country. By May 16, 3,348 COVID-19 cases - 48% of [[COVID-19 pandemic in Malaysia|Malaysia's total]] at the time - were linked to the event, and with approximately 10% of attendees visiting from overseas, the event resulted in the virus spreading across Southeast Asia. Cases in [[COVID-19 pandemic in Cambodia|Cambodia]], [[COVID-19 pandemic in Indonesia|Indonesia]], [[COVID-19 pandemic in Vietnam|Vietnam]], [[COVID-19 pandemic in Brunei|Brunei]], [[COVID-19 pandemic in the Philippines|the Philippines]] and [[COVID-19 pandemic in Thailand|Thailand]] were traced back to the mosque gathering.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Che Mat NF, Edinur HA, Abdul Razab MK, Safuan S | title = A single mass gathering resulted in massive transmission of COVID-19 infections in Malaysia with further international spread | journal = Journal of Travel Medicine | volume = 27 | issue = 3 | date = May 2020 | pmid = 32307549 | pmc = 7188142 | doi = 10.1093/jtm/taaa059 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-03-18|title=Wonder how dangerous a gathering can be? Here's how one event sparked hundreds of coronavirus cases across Asia|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-03-19/coronavirus-spread-from-malaysian-event-to-multiple-countries/12066092|access-date=2020-12-29|website=www.abc.net.au|language=en-AU}}</ref>

In [[COVID-19 pandemic in New York (state)|New York]], a lawyer contracted the illness then spread it to at least twenty other individuals in his community in [[New Rochelle]], creating a cluster of cases that quickly passed 100,<ref name="nycnn">{{cite web |author=Sheena Jones and Christina Maxouris |title=New York officials traced more than 50 coronavirus cases back to one attorney |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/03/11/us/new-rochelle-attorney-containment-area/index.html |website=CNN |date=11 March 2020 |access-date=13 March 2020}}</ref> accounting for more than half of SARS-CoV2 coronavirus cases in the state during early March 2020.<ref name="czcnn">{{cite web |author=Eric Levenson and Kristina Sgueglia |title=New York creates 'containment zone' around cluster of coronavirus cases in New Rochelle |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/03/10/us/new-rochelle-coronavirus/index.html |website=CNN |date=10 March 2020 |access-date=13 March 2020}}</ref> For comparison, the [[basic reproduction number]] of the virus, which is the average number of additional people that a single case will infect without any preventative measures, is between 1.4 and 3.9.<ref name="li20">{{cite journal | vauthors = Li Q, Guan X, Wu P, Wang X, Zhou L, Tong Y, Ren R, Leung KS, Lau EH, Wong JY, Xing X, Xiang N, Wu Y, Li C, Chen Q, Li D, Liu T, Zhao J, Liu M, Tu W, Chen C, Jin L, Yang R, Wang Q, Zhou S, Wang R, Liu H, Luo Y, Liu Y, Shao G, Li H, Tao Z, Yang Y, Deng Z, Liu B, Ma Z, Zhang Y, Shi G, Lam TT, Wu JT, Gao GF, Cowling BJ, Yang B, Leung GM, Feng Z | display-authors = 6 | title = Early Transmission Dynamics in Wuhan, China, of Novel Coronavirus-Infected Pneumonia | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 382 | issue = 13 | pages = 1199–1207 | date = March 2020 | pmid = 31995857 | pmc = 7121484 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMoa2001316 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="riou20">{{cite journal | vauthors = Riou J, Althaus CL | title = Pattern of early human-to-human transmission of Wuhan 2019 novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV), December 2019 to January 2020 | journal = Euro Surveillance | volume = 25 | issue = 4 | date = January 2020 | pmid = 32019669 | pmc = 7001239 | doi = 10.2807/1560-7917.ES.2020.25.4.2000058 }}</ref>

On March 6, preacher Baldev Singh returned to India after being infected while traveling in [[Italy]] and [[Germany]]. He subsequently died, becoming the first coronavirus fatality in the [[State of Punjab]]. Testing revealed that he'd infected 26 locals, including 19 relatives, while tracing discovered that he'd had direct contact with more than 550 people.<ref name=moose>{{Cite news|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/ludhiana/now-polices-moose-wala-song-blames-1st-casualty/articleshow/74859668.cms |title=Now, police's Moose Wala song blames 1st causality |date=2020-03-28|website=The Times of India|access-date=2020-08-17|language=en}}</ref> Fearing an outbreak, India's government instituted a local quarantine on 27 March 2020, affecting 40,000 residents from 20 villages.<ref name=bbcin>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-india-52061915 |title=India 'super spreader' quarantines 40,000 people|date=2020-03-27|work=BBC News|access-date=2020-03-27|language=en-GB}}</ref> Initial reports claimed that Baldev Singh had ignored self-quarantine orders, and police collaborated with singer [[Sidhu Moose Wala]] to release a [[Rapping|rap]] [[music video]] blaming the dead man for bringing the virus to Punjab. But Baldev Singh's fellow travelers insisted that no such order had been given, leading to accusations that local authorities had scapegoated him to avoid scrutiny of their own failures.<ref name="moose" /><ref name=vilified>{{Cite news|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/chandigarh/vilification-of-baldev-based-on-falsehood/articleshow/74882091.cms |title=Vilification of Baldev based on falsehood |date=2020-03-30|website=The Times of India|access-date=2020-08-17|language=en}}</ref>

A [[Tablighi Jamaat]] religious congregation that took place in Delhi's Nizamuddin Markaz Mosque in early March 2020 was a coronavirus super-spreader event, with more than 4,000 confirmed cases and at least 27 deaths linked to the event reported across the country. Over 9,000 missionaries may have attended the congregation, with the majority being from various states of India, and 960 attendees from 40 foreign countries. On 18 April, 4,291 confirmed cases of COVID-19 linked to this event by the Union Health Ministry represented a third of all the confirmed cases of India. Around 40,000 people, including Tablighi Jamaat attendees and their contacts, were quarantined across the country.{{citation needed|date=June 2021}}

On 11 May 2020, it came to light that a worker at a fish processing plant in [[Tema|Tema, Ghana]] was believed to have infected over 500 other people with COVID-19.<ref>{{cite web |author=Bukola Adebayo |title=A worker infected 533 others with coronavirus at a factory in Ghana, president says |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/05/11/africa/ghana-factory-coronavirus-infection-intl/index.html |website=CNN |date=11 May 2020 |access-date=11 May 2020 |quote=Hundreds of factory workers at a fish processing plant in Ghana have tested positive for the coronavirus, the country's president Nana Akufo-Addo said. All 533 of them contracted the virus from one worker at the factory in the port city of Tema, the president said in his public address to the nation Sunday.}}</ref>

As of 18 July 2020, more than one thousand suspected superspreading events had been logged, for example a cluster of 187 people who were infected after eating at a Harper's Restaurant and Brew Pub in East Lansing, Michigan.<ref>{{cite news | title='Superspreading' events, triggered by people who may not even know they are infected, propel coronavirus pandemic | vauthors = Cha A | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2020/07/18/coronavirus-superspreading-events-drive-pandemic/|newspaper=[[Washington Post]] | date=18 July 2020 | access-date=18 July 2020}}</ref>

On 26 September 2020, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his Supreme Court Justice nominee, [[Amy Coney Barrett]]. The announcement took place at the [[White House Rose Garden]], where around 30 people attentively watched. The [[White House COVID-19 outbreak|outbreak event]] has since been dubbed a "superspreader" event. Less than a week after the event, Trump himself was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2, as well as others who attended the Rose Garden event.<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors = Says AG |date=2020-11-02|title=Genomic sequence of the White House "superspreader" event|url=https://www.news-medical.net/news/20201102/Genomic-sequence-of-the-White-House-superspreader-event.aspx|access-date=2021-03-03|website=News-Medical.net|language=en}}</ref> By October 7, the [[Federal Emergency Management Agency]] memo revealed that 34 White House staff members, housekeepers, and other contacts had contracted the virus.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2020-10-10|title=White House hosted Covid 'superspreader' event, says Dr Fauci|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/election-us-2020-54487154|access-date=2021-03-03}}</ref>

The [[Kumbh Mela]] religious festival, which took place on 12 April 2021 in [[Haridwar]] in the state of [[Uttarakhand|Uttarkhand]] was considered to be a massive superspreader event that contributed to India's deadly second wave of COVID-19.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rocha | first1=I. C. | last2=Pelayo | first2=M. G. | last3=Rackimuthu | first3=S. | title=Kumbh Mela Religious Gathering as a Massive Superspreading Event: Potential Culprit for the Exponential Surge of COVID-19 Cases in India | journal=The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene | date=2021 | volume=105 | issue=4 | pages=868–871 | doi=10.4269/ajtmh.21-0601 | pmid=34460415 | pmc=8592171 }}</ref> 9.1 million pilgrims attended the festival, which coincided with a 1,800% increase in COVID-19 cases in Uttarkhand.<ref>{{cite web | title=India Covid: Kumbh Mela pilgrims turn into super-spreaders | date=9 May 2021 | url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-india-57005563 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Ellis-Petersen |first1=Hannah |last2=Hassan |first2=Aakash |date=30 May 2021 |title=Kumbh Mela: how a superspreader festival seeded Covid across India |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/may/30/kumbh-mela-how-a-superspreader-festival-seeded-covid-across-india |access-date=29 June 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

On 30 July 2021, it came to light that a Peruvian man, resident of [[Córdoba, Argentina]], brought the [[Delta variant]] of COVID-19 after travelling to Spain, but he did not quarantine himself, infecting 17 relatives and putting in isolation over 800 other people. He and three other people got arrested for disease propagation.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Ámbito I |title=A Peruvian man ignored Delta-variant positive, reunited with relatives and installed a "epidemiological bomb" on his town|url=https://www.ambito.com/informacion-general/covid-19/variante-delta-cordoba-ya-hay-mas-800-personas-aisladas-n5237191|website=Ámbito |access-date=9 August 2021 |quote= The Health's Ministry of Córdoba is intensively trying to detect and isolate that came in contact with the first Delta-variant infected in the province, that infected 17 relatives and threatened over more of 800 people}}</ref> 24 days later, the Peruvian man died of a severe pneumonia, being the first death of the Delta variant in Spain.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Perfil I |title=First death for Delta variant of Argentina: patient zero Peruvian man who infected his whole town died today |url= https://www.perfil.com/noticias/actualidad/primera-muerte-por-delta-en-argentina-fallecio-el-paciente-cero-de-cordoba.phtml |website= Perfil|date=22 August 2021 |access-date=23 August 2021 |quote= The same Peruvian man that started an "epidemiological bomb" on his town died from a severe pneumonia.}}</ref>

On 26 November 2021, [[Scatec|Scatec ASA]], a Norwegian company specializing in [[renewable energy]] systems, held a [[Christmas]] party in [[Oslo]], [[Norway]] attended by 120 people, all of whom were [[COVID-19 vaccine|fully vaccinated against COVID-19]] and tested negative for COVID-19 prior to the party being held. One person who attended the party had recently returned from [[South Africa]], the epicenter of the [[SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant|SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant outbreak]] and a country where the company has a [[solar panel]] project. It was later found that the attendee from South Africa had been infected with the Omicron variant. More than half of the party's attendees have since tested positive for COVID-19 and of those attendees, at least 13 of them were confirmed to have the variant.<ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Hinshaw D |date=2021-12-03|title=Omicron Cases at Norway Christmas Party Provide Clues on New Variant's Spread|language=en-US|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/omicron-cases-at-norway-christmas-party-provide-clues-on-new-variants-spread-11638554033|access-date=2021-12-03|issn=0099-9660}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Fouche G, Adomaitis N |date=2021-12-03|title=Omicron outbreak at Norway Christmas party is biggest outside S. Africa -authorities|language=en|work=[[Reuters]]|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/omicron-outbreak-norway-christmas-party-is-biggest-outside-s-africa-authorities-2021-12-03/|access-date=2021-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Erdbrink T, Libell HP, Frost N, Yoon J |date=2021-12-03|title=A Christmas party in Norway becomes a possible Omicron-spreading event, and other international news.|language=en-US|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/12/03/world/omicron-norway-christmas-party.html|access-date=2021-12-03|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

On 3 April 2022, the [[Gridiron Dinner]] in Washington D.C. led to at least 67 people testing positive for COVID-19, including three members of the [[Cabinet of Joe Biden]]: [[Merrick Garland]], [[Gina Raimondo]], and [[Tom Vilsack]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/67-attendees-test-positive-covid-high-profile-dc-dinner-rcna23763|title = 72 people at high-profile D.C. Dinner test positive for Covid|website = [[NBC News]]| date=10 April 2022 }}</ref>

In the [[SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant|later years of the COVID-19 pandemic]], concern has emerged that any large gatherings that take place without COVID-19 mitigation tools such as [[Mechanical filter (respirator)#Filtering facepiece respirators|respirator masks]] or [[Air filter|air filtration]] have the potential to become superspreader events.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Parramore |first=Lynn |date=May 31, 2024 |title=From Long COVID Odds to Lost IQ Points: Ongoing Threats You Don't Know About ===SARS outbreak: 2003===
[[File:Guangdong in China (+all claims hatched).svg|thumb|Guangdong Province in southeastern China where the first outbreak of SARS occurred in 2003.]]
The first cases of [[SARS]] occurred in mid-November 2002 in the [[Guangdong]] Province of China. This was followed by an outbreak in [[Hong Kong]] in February 2003. A Guangdong Province doctor, Liu Jianlun, who had treated SARS cases there, had contracted the virus and was symptomatic. Despite his symptoms, he traveled to Hong Kong to attend a family wedding. He stayed on the ninth floor of the Metropole Hotel in [[Kowloon]], infecting 16 other hotel guests also staying on that floor. The guests then traveled to Canada, Singapore, Taiwan, and Vietnam, spreading SARS to those locations and transmitting what became a global epidemic.<ref name=scielap>{{cite web|url=http://www.scielosp.org/pdf/bwho/v81n8/v81n8a14.pdf |title=How SARS changed the world in less than six months|access-date=February 4, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120405125444/http://www.scielosp.org/pdf/bwho/v81n8/v81n8a14.pdf |archive-date=April 5, 2012 }}</ref>

In another case during this same outbreak, a 54-year-old male was admitted to a hospital with coronary heart disease, chronic [[kidney failure]] and [[type II diabetes mellitus]]. He had been in contact with a patient known to have SARS. Shortly after his admission he developed fever, cough, myalgia and sore throat. The admitting physician suspected SARS. The patient was transferred to another hospital for treatment of his coronary artery disease. While there, his SARS symptoms became more pronounced. Later, it was discovered he had transmitted SARS to 33 other patients in just two days. He was transferred back to the original hospital where he died of SARS.{{citation needed|date=June 2021}}

In his post-mortem reflection, Low remained puzzled as to the reason for this phenomenon and speculated that "possible explanations for (the superspreaders') enhanced infectivity include the lack of early implementation of infection control precautions, higher load of SCoV, or larger amounts of respiratory secretions."<ref name=low04>{{cite book |last=Low |first=Donald |author-link=Donald Low |date=2004 |url= https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK92467/ |pages= 63–71 |title=Learning from SARS: Preparing for the Next Disease Outbreak: Workshop Summary|chapter=Sars: Lessons from Toronto |publisher=National Academies Press (US)}}</ref>

The SARS outbreak was eventually contained, but not before it caused 8,273 cases and 775 deaths. Within two weeks of the original outbreak in Guangdong Province, SARS had spread to 29 countries.<ref name="shen03"/>

===Measles outbreak: 1989===
[[File:Measles vaccination coverage world.svg|thumb|Rates of [[measles vaccine|measles vaccination]] worldwide in 2010]]
Measles is a highly contagious, air-borne virus that reappears even among vaccinated populations. In one Finnish town in 1989, an explosive school-based outbreak resulted in 51 cases, several of whom had been previously vaccinated. One child alone infected 22 others. It was noted during this outbreak that when vaccinated siblings shared a bedroom with an infected sibling, seven out of nine became infected as well.<ref name=paunio98>{{cite journal | vauthors = Paunio M, Peltola H, Valle M, Davidkin I, Virtanen M, Heinonen OP | title = Explosive school-based measles outbreak: intense exposure may have resulted in high risk, even among revaccinees | journal = American Journal of Epidemiology | volume = 148 | issue = 11 | pages = 1103–1110 | date = December 1998 | pmid = 9850133 | doi = 10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a009588 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Typhoid fever===
[[Typhoid fever]] is a human-specific disease caused by the bacterium   ''[[Salmonella typhi]]''. It is highly contagious and becoming resistant to antibiotics.<ref name=roger06>{{cite news|first = Roger | last = Highfield|title=Typhoid is with us to stay|publisher=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|date=28 November 2006|url= https://www.telegraph.co.uk/health/healthnews/3345526/Typhoid-is-with-us-to-stay.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110213072928/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/health/healthnews/3345526/Typhoid-is-with-us-to-stay.html |url-status= dead |archive-date= 13 February 2011 |access-date=2015-03-03}}</ref> ''S. typhi'' is susceptible to creating [[asymptomatic carrier]]s. The most famous carriers are [[Mary Mallon]], known as Typhoid Mary, from New York City, and Mr. N. the Milker, from Folkestone, England.<ref name="mortimer99">{{cite journal | vauthors = Mortimer PP | title = Mr N the milker, and Dr Koch's concept of the healthy carrier | journal = Lancet | volume = 353 | issue = 9161 | pages = 1354–1356 | date = April 1999 | pmid = 10218549 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(98)11315-6 | s2cid = 37788256 }}</ref> Both were active around the same time. Mallon infected 51 people from 1902 to 1909. Mr. N. infected more than 200 people over 14 years from 1901 to 1915. At the request of health officials, Mr. N. gave up working in food service. Mallon was at first also compliant, choosing other work – but eventually she returned to cooking and caused further outbreaks. She was involuntarily quarantined at [[North and South Brother Islands, East River|Brothers Island]] in New York, where she stayed until she died in November 1938, aged 69.<ref name="marr99">{{cite journal | vauthors = Marr JS | title = Typhoid Mary | journal = Lancet | volume = 353 | issue = 9165 | pages = 1714 | date = May 1999 | pmid = 10335825 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(05)77031-8 | s2cid = 1482311 }}</ref>

It has been found that ''Salmonella typhi'' persists in infected mice [[macrophages]] that have cycled from an inflammatory state to a non-inflammatory state. The bacteria remain and reproduce without causing further symptoms in the mice, and this helps to explain why carriers are asymptomatic.<ref name="ng13">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ng TM, Monack DM | title = Revisiting caspase-11 function in host defense | journal = Cell Host & Microbe | volume = 14 | issue = 1 | pages = 9–14 | date = July 2013 | pmid = 23870309 | pmc = 3785303 | doi = 10.1016/j.chom.2013.06.009 }}</ref><ref name="cox13">{{cite journal | vauthors = Eisele NA, Ruby T, Jacobson A, Manzanillo PS, Cox JS, Lam L, Mukundan L, Chawla A, Monack DM | display-authors = 6 | title = Salmonella require the fatty acid regulator PPARδ for the establishment of a metabolic environment essential for long-term persistence | journal = Cell Host & Microbe | volume = 14 | issue = 2 | pages = 171–182 | date = August 2013 | pmid = 23954156 | pmc = 3785333 | doi = 10.1016/j.chom.2013.07.010 }}</ref><ref name=mohanlat>{{cite news| vauthors = Mohan G |title=Typhoid Mary case may be cracked, a century later|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=August 14, 2013|url=https://www.latimes.com/science/sciencenow/la-sci-sn-typhoid-mary-20130814-story.html|access-date=2015-03-03}}</ref><ref name=mcneil13>{{cite news| vauthors = McNeil Jr DG |title= Bacteria study offers clues to Typhoid Mary mystery|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=August 26, 2013|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/27/health/bacteria-study-offers-clues-to-typhoid-mary-mystery.html?_r=0|access-date=2015-03-03}}</ref>
